1·Unbilled proceduresMeasured
$462K

a year in procedures that were done but never billed

“Nobody checks. There’s no report that compares what got done to what got billed.” Tom Kirkbride, IT Manager, May 20, 2025

procedures-monthly.csv·96 rows·above the 1.0% baseline, at the 78% collection rate

03 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. gap = procedures_completed - procedures_submitted_to_claim, per practice-month (procedures-monthly.csv).
  2. Baseline = sum of gaps / sum of completed at the 14 digital-handoff sites = 0.998%. Leakage at that rate happens anyway and is not counted.
  3. Excess per slip-site month = (gap - completed x baseline) x avg_procedure_value_usd; summed over the 96 slip-site rows = $592,915.44 of production.
  4. Annual net = excess x NET_COLLECTION 0.78 = $462,474.
  5. The split is clean: every slip-site month has a gap of at least 2.06%, every digital-site month at most 2.00%.
  6. Evidence: sum excess_value_usd over part = slip_site.

2·Denial queueModeled
$203K

a year from working denials by value, counted at the cautious end

5,033 of 17,089 denials age past the filing limit today. The saving runs $107K to $347K a year, depending on how much more work a big claim takes.

The queue has no sort by dollars or days left (SOP 3.2–3.3). The first month of the ranked queue measures the real effort curve.

claim-denials.csv·10,126 rows·row-average claim values

04 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. Per claim-denials row: average claim = denied_amount_usd / denied_claims; FIFO write-off = average x written_off_past_filing_limit = $1,299,671.88 on 5,033 claims (29.5% of denied claims); the P&L line is $1,300,094.73, the $423 gap is the pro-rata method. 'Provider not credentialed with payer' claims are held, not written off, and left out (see credential_hold).
  2. Effort: denial-worklog person-months, without the Senior AR Specialist (aged AR by phone, not the queue), fit touches = 1.043 + 0.00336 x value per recovered claim (n = 156, corr 0.39), at least 1 touch. The slope comes from differences between people: the 2 queue specialists average $124 a recovered claim and 1.14 touches, the others $214 and 1.82; within one person's months the slope is -0.0008.
  3. Capacity = resubmitted claims x touches at the row's average value = 21,475 touches. Worked highest value first until capacity runs out, 10,429 of the 16,303 claims are worked and 5,874 lost. Billed saved = $1,299,671.88 - $1,038,886.50 = $260,785.39; x NET_COLLECTION 0.78 = $203,413 counted.
  4. Upper bound, flat effort: the same 5,033 claims are lost, the cheapest ones ($854,994.76): $444,677 billed, $346,848 net. Sensitivity, slopes 0 to 0.005 through $256 at 1.75 touches: $107,331 to $346,848 net.
  5. Limits: row averages hide the spread inside a row; the effort line is fitted on person-month averages of $100 to $285 and extended to dearer claims; a value sort ignores days remaining (Medicaid 90 days, commercial 180, appeals 60).
  6. Evidence: sum fifo_writeoff_usd over all claim-denials rows; sum value_first_writeoff_usd (counted) and flat_writeoff_usd (upper) over part = pool; the fit uses part = effort_fit rows with in_fit = True.

benefits-enrollment.csv·18 rows

05 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. Predecessor plans = benefits-enrollment.csv rows whose plan_id starts with 'LEG'; their sponsoring_entity is the seller, not Northgate.
  2. All 18 people on a predecessor plan also hold an active Northgate plan, so the predecessor premium is pure duplication.
  3. Annual = sum of monthly_employer_premium_usd on the predecessor rows x 12 = $13,195.44 x 12 = $158,345.
  4. Sellers: Clearfork (2022), Riverbend (2021), Stonebridge (2024), Wabash (2024). HR's 2025-08-19 email names only Wabash and Stonebridge.
  5. Terminating a predecessor plan is the seller's obligation (benefits policy) and Northgate never verified it (appendix s10). Premiums already paid may be claimable from the sellers; that is not counted.
  6. Evidence: sum annual_employer_premium_usd over part = legacy_plan.

How this number was built

Method

  1. ap-ledger rows whose practice_id is neither in practices.csv nor CORP: NGD-23, NGD-24, 120 payments, $69,898.98 (Cintas, Dentrix, Spectrum Business, Vector Security, Weave, every month).
  2. Rows for NGD-23 and NGD-24 in operations-monthly, procedures-monthly, claims-monthly, employees: 0, so no production, patients or staff in FY2025. The Spectrum invoice shows NGD-23 service continuously active since 03/2023; the Vector statement shows no open/close activity at NGD-24.
  3. Halstead Creative Group 'Dayton market retainer' (CORP): 12 payments, $58,200.00. Practices in Dayton per practices.csv: 0. The only Dayton-area address in the packet is the NGD-24 Beavercreek site.
  4. Annual = $69,898.98 + $58,200.00 = $128,099.
  5. FY2026 plan: the services stop from 2026-03-01 (10 months, $58,249). Halstead renews each February unless cancelled 60 days ahead; the February 2026 renewal is assumed to stand, so FY2026 saves $0. The last day for notice on the next one falls between 2026-12-03 and 2026-12-30 (the MSA gives no day); notice by 2026-12-03 is safe.
  6. Also: $46,064 of these charges (Dentrix, Weave) are not in vendor-spend.csv, so the P&L software line does not show them. Evidence: sum amount_usd.

a year at the floor, up to $165K, from one distributor and every claim filed

Rebate income in the FY2025 P&L and AP ledger: $0

Schein share of purchase orders, every month: 49.5–50.6%

Counted at the floor: Patterson’s terms don’t say whether the rate covers the whole amount, and Schein pools only the sites on its Schedule A. For 2026, move volume to Patterson from March ($48K to $99K), compare item prices first, and rebid both at renewal.

purchase-orders.csv·1,860 rows·Schein agreement §7.2–7.3

07 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. 2025 POs: Henry Schein $1,503,335.21, Patterson $1,500,403.70, total $3,003,738.91; Henry Schein's monthly share runs 49.5% to 50.6%. At this split the rebates earned are $75,093 a year. No rebate income in the FY2025 P&L (0 rebate lines) or AP ledger ($0 of distributor credits).
  2. Counted floor = the lower of two cautious readings of all volume at one distributor: Patterson marginal (its summary does not say whole-amount) $73,937; Henry Schein without the sites acquired after the agreement, since only Schedule A locations aggregate (section 7.4) and Schedule A is not in the packet: $2,094,464 at the 4.0% tier = $83,779. Floor $73,937.
  3. Upper bound: Henry Schein on the whole amount (section 7.2) with every site listed, 5.5% x $3,003,739 = $165,206. Patterson on the whole amount would be $150,187.
  4. FY2026 (2025 months as the forecast; months before 2026-03-01 at the 2025 split): all volume to Patterson Dental from 2026-03-01 counts $2,476,975 of purchases to 2026-11-30: $47,829 on the marginal reading, up to $99,079 on the whole amount. Henry Schein instead gives $38,771 without the post-agreement sites on Schedule A, $88,989 with every site listed. Rebid both in Oct-Nov 2026 for a single-distributor renewal; Henry Schein's 5.5% whole-amount tier is the benchmark. Before moving volume, compare item prices on the preferred list: consolidation assumes the same prices at either distributor, which the packet cannot show.
  5. One-time, open at 2026-02-02: Henry Schein Q4-2025 $10,148, due 2026-02-14; Patterson FY2025 $12,510 (marginal reading; up to $37,510 whole-amount), due 2026-03-01; counted $22,658. Deadline passed (forfeited): Henry Schein Q1-2025, Henry Schein Q2-2025, Henry Schein Q3-2025.
  6. Evidence: sum amount_usd by distributor; HS Q4 = Henry Schein rows with quarter 4; Schedule A risk = rows with acquired_after_hs_agreement False.

payment-processing.csv·264 rows

08 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. Effective rate = sum of fees_usd / sum of volume_usd per processor (payment-processing.csv, 264 practice-months; each site uses one processor all year).
  2. Rates: Sunbit Merchant 2.422% (5 sites), BluePay Dental 2.913% (11 sites), CardConnect (legacy) 3.384% (6 sites).
  3. Saving = sum of (fees_usd - volume_usd x Sunbit rate) over the BluePay and CardConnect rows = $69,101 a year.
  4. vendor-spend.csv already carries Sunbit's SaaS fee at all 22 sites ($58,559 a year, contract to 2027-01-31), so the target platform is paid for.
  5. Not known: BluePay and CardConnect termination terms, and whether Sunbit's rate holds for the card mix at the other sites. Confirm both before counting the full amount.
  6. Evidence: sum savings_usd over part = card_volume.

claim-denials.csv·provider-roster.csv·procedures-monthly.csv·both supply agreements

09 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. claim-denials rows with reason 'Provider not credentialed with payer': 6 rows, all NGD-13 / Delta Dental, 2025-03 to 2025-08: 786 claims, $192,643.36, 0 resubmitted, 0 written off.
  2. provider-roster: PROV-024 Dr. Amara Osei, Delta Dental recredential_due 2025-02-01, credential_term 2025-03-14 (41 days later), reinstated 2025-08-22; denied dates of service run 2025-03-14 to 2025-08-21. Holding the claims was the RCM director's call; none has been resubmitted.
  3. Expected cash = billed x Delta Dental paid/submitted at NGD-13 in the 6 credentialed months (2025-01, 2025-02, 2025-09, 2025-10, 2025-11, 2025-12) = 0.85671 (sum paid / sum submitted, unrounded) = $165,040 while every window is open.
  4. Delta Dental allows rebilling for 365 days from the date of service, so windows close 2026-03-14 to 2026-08-21. At 2026-02-02, $192,643 of the $192,643 billed is inside its window ($165,040); 40 days to the first close.
  5. Rebilling is manual (plan module 0) because the first window closes 2026-03-14. Sweep, no dollars: 16 active provider-payer credentials (14 providers) were past their recredential date at 2026-02-02, 1 of them Medicaid (Dr. Orson Haddad at NGD-22), which allows no retroactive billing; 22 more fall due by 2026-05-03.
  6. Evidence: sum denied_amount_usd over part = held_claims; the ratio uses part = delta_paid_ratio rows with credentialed = True; the sweep is part = recredential_sweep. Dates of service are assumed evenly spread within each month.

Upside we’re not counting yet
$1.94M

a year from filling same-day openings, if a pilot proves it

Same-day openings rate

17,099 openings × 40% filled × $504 a visit × 78% collected × 72% margin = $1.94M

Fill rate has never been measured, and some filled slots only pull future visits forward. If managers already fill 20% of openings, the gain is about $969K. Pilot: 3 sites, 60 days.

operations-monthly.csv·appendix §6

14 / 15
How this number was built

Method

  1. Openings = no_shows + late_cancellations per practice-month (appendix section 13: treat the two together) = 17,099 in FY2025.
  2. Filled production = openings x FILL_RATE 0.4 (appendix section 6) x gross_production_usd / appointments_completed for that practice-month = $3,449,640.
  3. Contribution = production x NET_COLLECTION 0.78 x CONTRIBUTION_MARGIN 0.72 = $1,937,318. Not counted in the totals.
  4. Why not counted: today's fill rate is unmeasured (managers report 25-50% when they work the list), so part of this is already captured, and some fills pull demand forward rather than add visits. If 20% is filled today, the increment is $968,659.
  5. Openings run 21.7% of booked appointments at the 6 sites acquired since 2024 against 10.1% at the 16 legacy sites; NGD-22's first five months are ramp. Pilot at recent sites and measure first.
  6. Evidence: sum filled_production_usd and contribution_usd over all rows.

02System

One command. The deck’s exact numbers.

northgate-recovery reads the packet, computes all twelve findings in under two seconds, and writes out every row it used with its source file and line number. The deck and this page read one file it produces, so there’s no second copy of any number to drift.

Install and run, from a clone of northgate-recovery

$python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
$.venv/bin/python -m northgate

Python 3.10 or later. pandas is the only dependency. It installs into a local environment, so it works on a clean machine, and the run takes under two seconds.

Tests: .venv/bin/pip install pytest, then .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q
Also: explain <finding> · tieouts · plan · triage

03Documents

258,735 words. 27 worth reading.

Almost every line in the packet is one of a few hundred template sentences with a different town swapped in. Reading didn’t scale, and keyword search drowned in copies. So I stopped reading and started counting.

  1. 258,735words in 252 documents
  2. 185,361words of meetings, email and chat, in 15,908 lines
  3. 225sentence shapes once towns, names and numbers are masked
  4. 1,757words kept: 52 lines whose shape is rare, 99.1% removed

225 shapes cover all 15,908 lines. The filter keeps a line when its shape appears at most 2 times and it runs 12 words or more. Source: northgate/triage.py, run by python -m northgate triage.

Checking the filter

A filter that throws away 99% of the text needs its own check. A sub-agent read everything the filter dropped: all 142 unflagged emails in full, plus a separate normalization of every chat and transcript line. It found nothing I’d missed. It did find tells: every filler email is stamped 00:00:00, and eight serious-sounding decoy lines are each repeated 55 to 120 times. Citing one would’ve been a mistake.

What it missed, and how I caught it

v0 threw away quoted replies inside forwarded chains. One of them was Bev saying she’d been holding Dr. Osei’s denied Delta claims instead of writing them off. That’s the only evidence the money is still recoverable. I caught it because I read the flagged documents in full and didn’t trust the extracted lines. A test now checks that the line is kept.

04Harness

Specs pin the numbers. Agents have to disagree out loud.

One main session did the analysis and made the calls. Sub-agents took anything that could run in parallel or needed fresh eyes. There’s no custom infrastructure: the harness is the workflow. Specs that pin every number, agents that report a disagreement instead of fixing it, and one JSON contract between the system and the deck.

From analysis to deck, without retyping a number

The instruction that mattered most: report a number you think is wrong, don’t change it. It caught three mistakes.

  1. 102-analysis/findings_v0.py

    My first pass. One script, every number.

  2. 203-specs/SYSTEM-SPEC.md

    Pins every expected value. The agent reproduces them to the dollar and reports any it thinks are wrong.

  3. 3northgate-recovery

    The system: a CLI, evidence with source lines, 247 tests.

  4. 4deck-numbers.contract.json

    The only thing the deck may read. The system writes it; a test checks its shape.

  5. 505-deck/build.py

    Renders the slides from that JSON and exports the PDF. It rewrites a sentence before it types a number.

05Stress test

I tried to break my own numbers first

In Stage 3, Dana’s job is to disbelieve me, so I ran that meeting early. An agent with fresh context re-derived every headline from the raw CSVs before reading my code, then attacked the logic. Every number re-derived exactly. Two findings didn’t survive the logic, and they came down.

What changed because of it

FindingBeforeAfter
Denial queue$347K$203K counted, range $107K–$347K
Rebates$165K$74K floor, up to $165K
One-time$350K$318K: the backlog is now valued at go-live, not today
Headline$1.33M$1.10M counted, up to $1.33M

It also caught

  • Dr. Osei’s claims start expiring March 14, before the software that was supposed to rebill them goes live.
  • 16 provider-payer credentials are already past their recredential date, one of them Medicaid (no retro billing). That’s the same setup as the Osei lapse.
  • “Sites that never opened” is stronger than the evidence. The IT manager thought they opened in 2023.

A second opinion on the first opinion

When the system agent implemented the effort-adjusted model, it pointed out something important. The effort slope comes from differences between people: the two queue specialists work cheap claims fast. Within one person’s months, the slope is flat. So “bigger claims take more work” isn’t proven either.

I kept the cautious number as the counted floor and put the full range on the slide. The first month of the ranked queue measures the real effort curve. That’s the honest version: I don’t know the slope, the data doesn’t know it, and the pilot finds out.

Six questions I expect in Stage 3

With the answer the data supports after the revisions.

“Why would value-first ordering lose the same number of claims if big claims take more work?”

It might not. That’s why the counted number is the cautious $203K, not $347K. Within one person’s work, the data shows no effort slope. The ranked queue’s first month measures it.

“Are Wabash and Stonebridge on Schein’s Schedule A?”

We don’t know. The floor ($74K) doesn’t depend on it. For 2026 we’d move volume to Patterson, which has no Schedule A clause, and rebid both at renewal.

“How much of the $1.10M is measured, not modeled?”

$818K. That’s unbilled procedures, duplicate plans, ghost spend and card fees. Denials ($203K) are modeled. Rebates ($74K) are contractual, at the floor.

“What does a month’s delay cost?”

The $10K Schein claim (Feb 14) and the Patterson claim (Mar 1). About $1,200 a day of unbilled backlog. And Dr. Osei’s claims start expiring Mar 14.

“Can we get back what we already paid on the sellers’ plans?”

Maybe. It’s the sellers’ obligation under the purchase agreements, and FY2025 alone was $158K. That’s counsel’s call, and it isn’t counted.

“Isn’t your $1.94M backfill just Grantley again?”

That’s why it isn’t counted. If managers already fill 20% of openings, it’s about $969K. Nothing counts until a 3-site pilot measures the fill rate.

06What broke

Ten things broke. Here’s how each one got caught.

In the order they happened. Every one of them would’ve reached the deck if nothing had checked it.

  1. 01The document filter dropped quoted repliesCaught by reading the flagged documents in full, then by the system agent.

    What happened. v0 of the filter (01-triage/detemplate_v0.py) splits each email into paragraphs and skips any paragraph that starts with a header line. In a forwarded chain every quoted reply starts with > From:. So the filter threw away whole replies, including Bev’s line about holding Dr. Osei’s Delta claims instead of writing them off. That line is the only proof those claims are still recoverable.

    How I caught it. Not with the filter. I read the flagged documents in full, and the Toledo thread’s subject line and first paragraph were enough to open it. Later the system-builder agent tried to cite Bev’s quote from python -m northgate triage and noticed it wasn’t in the output.

    Fix. Strip the quote markers first, then drop only the header lines inside each quoted block and keep the body. A test now asserts Bev’s line is in the triage output. The lesson: a filter tuned to throw away repetition will also throw away structure, so I spot-read what it keeps and what it drops.

  2. 02Sentence-initial place names beat the skeletonCaught when the flagged list showed lines I’d already seen with other towns in them.

    What happened. The skeleton masks capitalized words, but it skipped the first word of an utterance so that normal sentences survive. The template lines start with a place (“Florence had a patient complaint about wait times”), so each place name produced a “unique” line. v0 flagged 43 documents. 30 of them were filler.

    How I caught it. The flagged list had lines I’d already seen repeated with different towns.

    Fix. Mask every place name from practices.csv (plus Columbus and Dayton) wherever it appears. Flagged documents dropped from 43 to 13, and the 13 are exactly the real ones.

  3. 03The 8 “manual” sites aren’t the ones the appendix describesCaught in the per-site gap rates. The data and Tom agree; the appendix doesn’t.

    What happened. The appendix says the 8 routing-slip sites are “the 2024 and later acquisitions”. Only 6 sites were acquired in 2024 or later. My first pass would have used those 6.

    How I caught it. Per-site gap rates in procedures-monthly.csv. The top 8 match Tom Kirkbride’s list from the May 20 IT call exactly, and that list includes Florence (2022) and Nicholasville (2023). The data and Tom agree; the appendix is the one that’s wrong. It’s on the “where the documents disagree” slide now.

  4. 04I nearly counted the wrong rebate contractCaught by the system agent, because its prompt said report, don’t fix.

    What happened. My first spec counted Patterson at 5.0% of the whole amount as the “conservative” rebate. The system-builder agent pointed out that Patterson’s summary never says whether the rate applies to the whole amount or only the portion above each tier. On the marginal reading it’s $73,937, not $150,187. The Henry Schein agreement says it explicitly: “applied to the entirety of Net Purchases, not marginally”.

    Fix. Count Schein at 5.5% ($165,206). Book Patterson’s 2025 claim on the marginal reading ($12,510) and show $37,510 as the upper bound. The prompt told the agent to report disagreements instead of silently changing numbers, and that’s the only reason this surfaced.

  5. 05Rounding before multiplying$55 on $165K. The brief says the same numbers, so it’s fixed.

    The Delta paid ratio was rounded to 0.857 before it was applied. That’s $55 on $165K. Nobody would notice, but the brief says “not similar numbers, the same ones”, so it now uses the unrounded ratio.

  6. 06“Lowest in the company” wasn’t trueCaught when the agent ranked everyone, not just the full-time staff.

    The first report said Marguerite Vance had the lowest on-site hours in the company. She’s the lowest of the 171 full-time staff; 59 part-timers log fewer. The agent caught it by actually ranking everyone. The slide says “lowest of 171 full-time staff”.

  7. 07“Ranked by dollars” stopped being trueCaught reviewing slide 2 at full size. A test now enforces the order.

    When the rebate moved from $150K to $165K, it passed duplicate health plans ($158K). The slide title still said “ranked by dollars” and the order was wrong. I caught it reviewing slide 2 at full size, and the agent flagged the same thing. Ranks are now computed from value, and a test enforces the order.

  8. 08Liquid glass disappears in PDFCaught diffing the screen against the PDF, pixel by pixel.

    What happened. CSS backdrop-filter is ignored when Chromium prints. The glass came out as flat panels with a sharp grid showing through. A blurred copy of the background escaped its clip and covered the text.

    Fix. Bake it. Render each slide at 2x with all the text hidden, and put that image under the slide as the background. Then print the text and charts as live vector on top. The glass matches pixel for pixel, and every word is still selectable. The comparison of all four approaches is in 05-deck/glass-kit/NOTES.md and lab.html.

  9. 09The first deck spec asked for numbers that don’t existCaught by the deck agent refusing to type a number the contract didn’t have.

    My deck spec had copy like “6 sites acquired since 2024” and “Corporate headcount stays at 31”. Those numbers weren’t in the JSON contract. The deck agent refused to type them in by hand and reworded the copy instead. That was annoying in the moment and correct: every figure on a slide has to come out of the system.

  10. 10The fonts I picked couldn’t be installedFixed by committing to Instrument Sans, not by routing around the network.

    What happened. The deck was designed around Inter and Inter Tight. This build environment blocks Google Fonts, npm and GitHub, so Inter was never available offline for the PDF. The drafts rendered in a stand-in, and the web version would have loaded Inter from Google at view time. That meant two different typefaces for one deck.

    Fix. I didn’t route around the network policy. I committed to the stand-in on purpose: Instrument Sans (OFL), which ships with the glass kit. It has the precision and tabular figures I wanted from Inter, with more character at display sizes. The PDF embeds it, and the web page carries the same four weights inline, so every surface shows the exact same letters.
